opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is really the heart of what we were getting at in the "mirage" work. When people looked at arithmetic tasks, like multi-digit addition or multiplication, the standard metric was exact match: either the model gets every digit of the answer right or it gets zero credit. That's a very harsh, very nonlinear way of scoring. If you think about it, even if the model's per-token accuracy is improving smoothly and predictably as you scale up, the probability of getting, say, five digits all correct is roughly that per-token accuracy raised to the fifth power. So on a plot it looks flat near zero for a long time, and then it shoots up. That looks like a sudden, sharp transition, and it's easy to call it emergence.

But when we took the same model outputs and scored them with a continuous metric, like token edit distance or per-token accuracy, a lot of those sharp jumps turned into smooth, fairly predictable curves. Nothing about the models changed. Only the measuring stick changed.

So my takeaway is that the metric is part of the claim. If you say a model has an emergent capability, you're really saying something about the model *plus* how you chose to measure it. A few practical implications follow from that.

First, look at multiple metrics, especially continuous ones, before you conclude something is discontinuous. If the jump only shows up under a discontinuous or thresholded metric, that's a red flag that you might be seeing an artifact.

Second, resolution matters. If you only evaluate on a small test set, you can't distinguish an accuracy of, say, 0.1% from 0%, so small models look like they can't do the task at all. Using larger test sets gives you the resolution to see the gradual improvement that's actually happening.

Third, be clear about why you picked the metric. Sometimes exact match is genuinely what you care about. If I'm using a model to do arithmetic for my taxes, being off by one digit is a failure, and it's fair to say the *useful* capability shows up abruptly. That's a legitimate statement. It's just a different statement than "the model's underlying competence changed discontinuously with scale."

And I want to be careful here, because people sometimes read our work as saying emergence never happens. That's not the claim. The claim is that a lot of what's been reported as emergent can be explained by metric choice, so the burden is on us as researchers to rule that out before making strong claims. That matters a lot for things like safety and forecasting. If capabilities really appear unpredictably, that's scary and hard to plan for. If they're actually improving smoothly and we're just measuring them in a way that hides it, then we have a much better shot at anticipating what bigger models will do.

r001.rationale: It says exact-match scoring can make smooth improvement look like a sudden emergence, while continuous metrics reveal smoother curves; the metric materially affects the conclusion.

r002.rationale: It says an emergence claim describes the model plus the chosen measuring method and distinguishes apparent metric-driven transitions from changes in underlying competence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the heart of the argument we made in the "mirage" paper. When people say a model has an emergent ability in arithmetic, what they usually mean is that performance is essentially zero across a range of model scales, and then at some scale it jumps up sharply and unpredictably. And that's a striking claim, because it suggests you can't forecast what a bigger model will do.

But if you look carefully at how those claims are made, almost all of them rely on a metric like exact match accuracy. For a multi-digit addition problem, you get credit only if every single digit in the output is correct. And that metric is nonlinear in a very specific way: if the model's per-token accuracy improves smoothly with scale, say it goes from 80 percent to 90 percent to 95 percent per digit, then the probability of getting all five or ten digits right goes from something close to zero to something meaningfully above zero in a way that looks discontinuous. The sharpness is a product of the metric, not necessarily of the model.

So what we did is take the same models, the same outputs, and just swap the metric. If you use something like edit distance, or token-level accuracy, which gives partial credit, that cliff goes away. You see smooth, predictable improvement with scale. The model's underlying competence is changing gradually; the exact match metric is what's hiding that from you.

The implication for how you should make claims is, I think, pretty direct. If you're going to say something is emergent, you have a responsibility to ask whether the emergence survives a change in how you measure. Is the discontinuity in the model, or in the lens you're pointing at it? And relatedly, you need enough test data. A lot of these benchmarks have small evaluation sets, so when accuracy is near zero, you're estimating a tiny quantity with very few samples, and small models just look like they're flat at zero when really they're at one or two percent and improving.

I want to be careful here, because I don't think this means nothing interesting happens with scale, or that no capability can ever appear sharply. There may be real cases. But the burden of proof should be higher than "we picked a harsh metric and saw a jump." Pick the metric that reflects what you actually care about, be explicit that your choice has consequences for the shape of the curve, and ideally report multiple metrics so readers can see whether the phenomenon is robust. Otherwise you're making a claim about the model that's really a claim about your scoring function.

r001.rationale: It explains that exact-match scoring can make smooth improvements appear as a sharp emergence, while partial-credit metrics reveal gradual improvement; the metric therefore affects conclusions about emergence.

r002.rationale: It cautions that an apparent jump may come from the scoring function rather than the model, and recommends checking robustness across metrics before making claims about model behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be very careful about distinguishing emergence in the underlying capability from emergence in the metric. Take arithmetic: if you score an answer as correct only when every digit is right, that’s a very sharp threshold. A model might be improving gradually in how many digits it gets right, but your exact-match score stays close to zero until suddenly it starts producing fully correct answers. That can look like a capability appeared out of nowhere.

If you instead measure digit-level accuracy, you may see a much smoother progression. Neither metric is necessarily wrong. If you need the correct answer to use the system, exact match is quite meaningful. But it supports a different claim from saying the model’s underlying ability changed abruptly.

So I’d want to look at several complementary metrics and ask whether the apparent transition persists. The metric is part of the observation, and we shouldn’t automatically attribute its sharpness to the model.

r001.rationale: The response explains that exact-match scoring can make gradual arithmetic improvement look like sudden emergence, while digit-level accuracy shows a smoother progression.

r002.rationale: It warns that a metric’s apparent sharpness should not automatically be attributed to the model, and that exact-match results support a different claim about underlying ability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be very careful about distinguishing emergence in the model from emergence in the metric. Take arithmetic: if you score an answer as correct only when every digit is correct, you might see performance stay near zero and then suddenly jump as you scale the model. But if you measure how many digits it gets right, you may see steady improvement over that same range.

The exact-match metric can be perfectly reasonable if what you care about is getting the whole calculation right. But that sharp jump alone doesn’t establish that the model suddenly acquired a new capability. It could be gradual improvement passing through a fairly unforgiving scoring rule.

So I’d want to see the claim tested across reasonable metrics, including ones that capture partial progress. If the discontinuity depends on the metric, that tells us to qualify the claim: we’ve observed a sharp change in measured task success, but we haven’t necessarily demonstrated a sharp change in the underlying capability.

r001.rationale: It contrasts exact-match scoring, which can show a sudden jump, with digit-level scoring, which can show steady improvement, and says the discontinuity may depend on the metric.

r002.rationale: It cautions that a sharp change in measured task success does not establish a sharp change in underlying capability, and recommends qualifying the claim based on the metric.
